The method controls the non-productive movement of a tool from a defined starting position to a defined end position within the travel envelope of a machine tool. As an initial basis, a collision-free first trajectory is provided. This trajectory comprises multiple rectilinear segments connecting the starting and end positions.

An algorithm then determines a second trajectory that includes at least one polynomial segment. The second trajectory is optimized according to a selectable target parameter, such as travel time, path length, or another relevant motion criterion. Following optimization, the second trajectory is checked for possible collisions within the machine tool’s travel envelope.

If the collision check confirms that the second trajectory is collision-free, a corresponding instruction is generated or provided to control the tool’s movement along that trajectory. If a collision is detected, however, the model of the travel envelope is modified. The optimization and collision-checking steps are then repeated using the modified model until a collision-free second trajectory is obtained.

The method controls non-productive movement of a machine tool, such as travel between two machining operations during which no material is removed. First, a collision-free trajectory is determined between a starting position and a target position. This initial trajectory comprises multiple rectilinear segments and is calculated with reference to a travel-envelope model representing obstacles, machine components, workpieces, fixtures, and other regions that the moving tool or machine element must avoid.

The multi-segment trajectory is then processed by an optimization algorithm. The algorithm replaces or approximates the rectilinear segments with a polynomial trajectory while optimizing at least one selected target parameter. Depending on the application, the target parameter may include travel time, path length, velocity, acceleration, jerk, energy consumption, or a combination of these factors. The resulting polynomial trajectory provides smoother transitions than the original segmented path and can reduce abrupt changes in direction, thereby improving movement efficiency and reducing mechanical loading on the machine.

After optimization, the polynomial trajectory is checked for collisions using the travel-envelope model. The collision check may account for the dimensions and orientation of the tool, spindle, tool holder, machine axes, or any other component that moves along or near the trajectory. If the optimized trajectory remains within an allowable movement region and does not intersect an obstacle, a corresponding movement instruction is generated and transmitted to the machine-tool controller for execution.

If a collision or an unacceptable clearance is detected, the travel-envelope model is modified to reflect the problematic region. For example, the model may be expanded around an obstacle, supplemented with an additional exclusion region, or otherwise adjusted to force the next trajectory away from the detected collision. The rectilinear path and/or the polynomial trajectory is then recalculated using the modified model. This optimization and collision-checking cycle may be repeated until a collision-free polynomial trajectory satisfying the selected target parameter and any applicable machine constraints is obtained.

In this way, the method combines the reliability of collision-free rectilinear path planning with the efficiency and smoothness of polynomial trajectory optimization. The iterative use of a modified travel-envelope model enables the system to avoid unsafe solutions while progressively identifying a feasible route, resulting in safer, faster, and less mechanically demanding non-productive machine-tool travel.

### The Power of “The”

“The” is one of the smallest and most frequently used words in the English language. Although it may seem unimportant, it plays an essential role in communication. As a definite article, “the” identifies a specific person, place, object, or idea. For example, saying “the book” points to a particular book rather than any book.

This simple word helps create clarity and shared understanding. It can also give something a sense of uniqueness, as in “the truth,” “the future,” or “the world.” Without “the,” many English sentences would sound incomplete or unclear.

Sometimes, the most ordinary words carry the greatest responsibility. “The” reminds us that even a tiny element can make a meaningful difference.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style abstract for a method that optimizes non-productive tool movement in a machine tool while repeatedly checking for collisions.
counterfactuals.output: A computer-implemented method for optimizing non-productive movement of a tool in a machine tool is disclosed. The method includes receiving a tool path comprising productive motion segments and non-productive motion segments, determining an initial trajectory for at least one non-productive motion segment, and iteratively modifying the initial trajectory to reduce a travel time, travel distance, or machine-axis movement. After each modification, the method performs a collision check using digital models of the tool, a workpiece, fixtures, and at least a portion of the machine tool. A modified trajectory is accepted when the collision check indicates that required clearances are maintained and an optimization criterion is improved, and is rejected or further modified when a collision is detected. The modifying and collision-checking operations are repeated until a termination condition is satisfied. The resulting collision-free trajectory is incorporated into machine instructions for controlling the machine tool, thereby reducing non-productive operating time while maintaining collision avoidance.

counterfactuals.output: A method for controlling non-productive movement of a machine tool from a start position to an end position comprises determining at least one candidate trajectory for a movable machine component, optimizing the candidate trajectory according to a predefined criterion, including travel time, path length, energy consumption, or axis loading, and simulating movement along the optimized trajectory using a geometric model of the machine tool, workpiece, fixtures, and surrounding interference regions. The optimized trajectory is subjected to collision checking over the complete movement, including intermediate positions and machine-axis constraints. Only when the trajectory is determined to be collision-free is the trajectory converted into a corresponding machine-tool instruction, such as a numerical-control rapid-traverse command or sequence of axis commands, and supplied to the machine controller for execution. If a collision or constraint violation is detected, conversion is inhibited and an alternative trajectory is generated and evaluated.
